records.sourceFile: Implementing exposure limits for players in contact team sports - Review of principles and practices.pdf

paper.citation: Fuller CW. Implementing exposure limits for players in contact team sports: review of principles and practices. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2025;7:1593766.
paper.abstract: This mini review applies occupational exposure-limit principles to professional contact team sports such as football and rugby union. It covers how workplace limits are defined, the criteria for prescribing occupational disease, and the evidence on post-career neurological disease and knee osteoarthritis. The author concludes that current evidence cannot confirm or reject these health concerns, and recommends research designed to support evidence-based sport exposure limits.
paper.tldr: Post-career neurological disease and knee osteoarthritis in contact sport players are not confirmed as occupational health concerns, so current exposure limits are precautionary. The author recommends research designed to meet occupational health criteria before limits are set.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described systematic search. The author reviews UK occupational health principles for workplace exposure limits and the criteria for prescribing occupational disease, then considers the evidence on post-career health in professional football and rugby players.
paper.findings: Studies of retired UK professional players have reported more lower-limb osteoarthritis in footballers and more neurological disease in rugby and football players than in the general population, but three Industrial Injuries Advisory Council reviews judged the evidence insufficient to prescribe these conditions as occupational diseases. Two studies of retired footballers suggested a possible exposure-response relationship between heading and neurological concerns, but the author judges that no study alone was sufficient to confirm exposure-related health concerns or set limits. The 30 game-involvement season limit in English professional rugby from 2024/25 was based on a study that found no association between previous-season match exposure and current-season match injury incidence, and the 10 high-force headers per week limit in English football was introduced under the Precautionary Principle.
paper.limitations: The author notes that few sport-related studies were designed to examine post-career health, and that definitions of osteoarthritis vary across studies, which limits cross-study comparison. The review gives no search strategy, and it does not establish exposure limits or their effect on long-term health.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat sport exposure limits as policy decisions rather than evidence-confirmed requirements, since the author states that the evidence cannot confirm or reject the health concerns. Record training and match exposures alongside injury data in a consistent format, because the author argues that this would help future studies test exposure-response relationships. Present exposure caps as policy decisions when discussing them with players or staff.
paper.athleteDev: Sport exposure limits, such as the game-involvement and heading limits discussed, are policy decisions rather than established performance or load standards. The author argues that consistent exposure data would help future studies set evidence-based limits, so collecting such data is worthwhile now.
paper.rtp: This review does not address injury rehabilitation or return-to-play criteria. Its discussion of injury burden and post-career health concerns does not support any clearance decision for injured players.
